status: complete — selective in the law code and the conquest material; see coverage_note; awaiting second-pass review
note: The Two Ways in its original form, upstream of both the Didache and C01. Indexed in sections along the book's own seams: the first address and the history (1-4), the second address with the Decalogue and the Shema (5-11), the law code (12-26), the blessings, curses, and covenant renewal (27-30), and the song and death of Moses (31-34). All five sections are indexed.
sectioning_note: As with Jeremiah, sectioning is a practical necessity and the status field names what is done. The prior citations the Scriptural Appendix makes for this book — 18:15, 30:19, 32:4, and the gleaning, wage, and honest-scale laws — are all carried: 18:15, 24:10-15, 24:17-22, and 25:13-16 in the law code, 30:15-20 and 32:1-14 in the closing chapters.
coverage_note: Chapters 1-11, unindexed by decision: the destruction of Sihon and Og with 'the women and the little ones' (2:24-3:11), the allotment of the eastern lands (3:12-17), the summary at 4:44-49, and the command to destroy the seven nations and show them no mercy, with the blessings and assurances bound up in it (7:1-5, 7:12-26: 'your eye shall not pity them'). These are among the hardest texts in the canon for a curriculum built on mercy, and the index does not soften them by allegory — including the long monastic tradition of reading 7:22, 'by little and little,' as the gradual conquest of the passions — nor tag them by stretching. WMT's genealogy nowhere adopts an allegorical hermeneutic, as noted for the Song of Solomon. They are recorded here as left out, not as judged to be of no weight; a reader of the curriculum will meet them, and the index should not pretend they are absent. Chapters 12-26, the law code, are indexed selectively, as Jeremiah 46-52 was. Left out: the destruction of the nations' shrines (12:1-4) and the blood and meat regulations (12:20-28); the death penalties for enticement and apostasy and the destruction of an apostate town (13:5-18, 17:2-7); the food laws (14:1-21); the firstborn and blemished-sacrifice rules (15:19-23, 17:1) and the central court (17:8-13); the landmark law (19:14); the war laws, including the herem of 20:16-18 (20:10-20); the captive woman (21:10-14); the stoning of a rebellious son and the hanged man (21:18-23); the laws of clothing, mixed seed, and fringes (22:5-12); the sexual and marriage laws of 22:13-30 and the divorce law of 24:1-4, which Jesus addresses directly in Matthew 19 and which are better indexed there; the assembly exclusions (23:1-6), camp purity (23:9-14), cult prostitution and interest (23:17-20) and the passer-by's right to eat (23:24-25); the millstone pledge, kidnapping, and leprosy laws (24:6-9) and individual responsibility (24:16); the ox unmuzzled (25:4); the woman's hand (25:11-12); and the command to blot out Amalek (25:17-19). Some of these are humane and some are among the hardest laws in the Torah; what they share is that they anchor nothing in a curriculum of personal formation without allegory or a stretched tag. In chapters 27-34, the tribal blessings of 33:1-25 and 33:28-29 are left out for the same reason.
prediction_note: The indexing order called Deuteronomy 'the Two Ways in its original form, upstream of both the Didache and C01,' with 30:15-20 as its centre. The Two Ways is reached four times — 11:26-32, 28:1-14, 28:15-68, and 30:15-20 — and the last carries PR07, the Daily Anchors, whose morning sentence is drawn from it. The drafter did not forecast that the book would also be the densest single source for Habitual Almsgiving yet indexed: eight entries carry PR05, three of them on the Scriptural Appendix's own citations.

entries.pericope: You have lived long enough in this mountain
entries.connection: The book opens at the edge of the land, forty years late, with the instruction given at Horeb repeated: 'You have lived long enough in this mountain: turn, and take your journey.' The place of revelation is not the place to stay. C25's growth by steps, in which each stage is left for the next, has its first image here.

entries.pericope: You shall hear the small and the great alike
entries.connection: Moses admits he cannot bear the people alone and distributes the burden, and the charge to the judges is the first statement of the book's justice: judge between a man and his brother 'and the foreigner who is living with him,' without partiality, 'the small and the great alike,' unafraid of any face, 'for the judgment is God's.' Authority shared rather than hoarded, and held for the weak in the case, is C16's account of what authority is for.

entries.pericope: We have sinned… we will go up and fight
entries.connection: Two failures in sequence. At Kadesh the people refuse the land and explain their fear by reading the worst motive into God — 'Because Yahweh hated us, he has brought us forth' — a misdiagnosis of the kind C21 traces to its root, against the record of a God who 'bore you, as a man does bear his son.' Then, told they will not enter, they say 'We have sinned' and go up to fight after all, against an explicit command, and are routed. The confession is turned into a bid to reverse the consequence rather than a return to the obedience actually asked, which was to turn back into the wilderness. The Failure Recovery Protocol asks for exactly the ordinary next act of obedience, without ceremony; this is what its absence looks like when it is dressed as repentance.

entries.pericope: Don't contend with them… you have lacked nothing
entries.connection: Three peoples are to be passed by and not fought — Esau, Moab, Ammon — because their land was given to them, and Israel is to pay for its food and water. Esau is named 'your brothers.' Restraint toward kin who are also rivals is C15's ground, and the reason given for being content to buy rather than take — 'these forty years Yahweh your God has been with you; you have lacked nothing' — is C18's.

entries.pericope: Until Yahweh gives rest to your brothers, as to you
entries.connection: The tribes who have already received their land east of the Jordan are to cross armed ahead of the others and not return home until their brothers have rest as well. Their own settlement is deferred until the others are settled. C13's ordinary faithfulness to a shared life, as a condition of enjoying one's own portion. PR26 does not apply: the obligation is commanded, not unobligated.

entries.pericope: Let it suffice you; speak no more to me of this matter
entries.connection: Moses pleads to see the land and is refused: 'Let it suffice you.' He is allowed to see it from Pisgah and told to spend what remains on strengthening Joshua, who will go where he cannot. The refusal is accepted and the energy turned to a successor. Detachment from the one thing he had worked forty years toward, C18, issuing in the logic of service, C16.

entries.pericope: Take heed to yourself, and keep your soul diligently
entries.connection: The statutes are called 'your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the peoples,' wisdom as a way of living that can be seen, which is C02's definition. 'Keep your soul diligently, lest you forget… and lest they depart from your heart' uses the keeping of the heart that C20 takes from Proverbs 4:23, and the remedy for forgetting is to teach it to one's children, which is C14's household. PR12 shares the guard but its object here is memory rather than the arriving thought, so it is not tagged.

entries.pericope: You saw no kind of form
entries.connection: The prohibition of images is grounded in what was and was not seen at Horeb: a voice, and no form. God is not to be reduced to a likeness that can be held. C24's discipline of wonder rests on the same refusal, though the curriculum's PR04 concerns mental grasp rather than images and is not tagged here. The paragraph ends in exile and return: 'from there you shall seek Yahweh your God, and you shall find him, when you search after him with all your heart… for Yahweh your God is a merciful God.' C19's door, opened from the far country.

entries.pericope: Know therefore this day, and lay it to your heart
entries.connection: Ask of all the days since creation whether anything like this has happened. The argument moves from what was seen to what is to be known — 'Yahweh he is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is none else' — and from that to keeping the statutes 'that it may go well with you.' C01's reality with a grain: the commandments are given as fitted to the way things are.

entries.pericope: The manslayer… who didn't hate him in time past
entries.connection: Cities of refuge for one who kills his neighbour 'unawares, and didn't hate him in time past.' The law distinguishes the act from the heart that produced it, which is C21's distinction between a visible failure and its root, and it provides a door for the one whose harm did not come from hatred — C19's mercy given an address.

entries.pericope: Not with our fathers, but with us, who are all of us here alive this day
entries.connection: The covenant is made not with a past generation but 'with us, even us, who are all of us here alive this day,' and the first words are the reason before the rule: 'I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out… out of the house of bondage.' The commandments as the shape of a freedom already given, which is how C01 presents the moral order — not imposed on reality but describing it.

entries.pericope: That your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you
entries.connection: Deuteronomy's sabbath differs from Exodus's in its reason. Here it is so that the servant, the stranger, even the ox may rest 'as well as you,' and 'you shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt.' The household's rhythm is set for the benefit of its weakest members, by a people told to remember being the weakest. C16's why-the-vulnerable-specifically, kept inside C14's home.

entries.pericope: Neither shall you covet
entries.connection: The second table, ending in a command against a desire rather than an act: 'neither shall you covet… neither shall you desire your neighbor's house.' The moral order reaches inward to the movement before the deed, which is C20's territory. PR12 shares the subject but the commandment forbids the movement without prescribing the attention by which it is caught, so it is not tagged.

entries.pericope: Oh that there were such a heart in them
entries.connection: Afraid of the fire, the people ask for a mediator, and God approves the request — the arrangement that 18:15 will extend into the promise of a prophet like Moses, C08's True Prophet. Then a sentence of longing from God's side: 'Oh that there were such a heart in them, that they would fear me.' The change of heart that C26 promises through Ezekiel is first wished for here.

entries.pericope: When you lie down, and when you rise up
entries.connection: The Shema: Yahweh is one, and love him with all your heart, soul, and might. Then the means, which are entirely ordinary — on your heart, taught to your children, spoken of 'when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.' A love sustained by being returned to at fixed points in the day. The Daily Anchors set the day between a morning choice and an evening review, and this is their oldest form. Confidence is medium because the passage commands keeping the words present across the day rather than the Anchors' specific morning, midday, and evening content; PR30's fixed-hour prayer is the Lord's Prayer and is not tagged.

entries.pericope: Houses full of all good things, which you didn't fill
entries.connection: Cities you didn't build, houses you didn't fill, cisterns you didn't dig, vineyards you didn't plant — 'and you shall eat and be full; then beware lest you forget.' Abundance named as the danger rather than the reward. C18's warning, and the remedy is C10's: remembering who gave it.

entries.pericope: When your son asks you in time to come
entries.connection: The child's question — what do all these commands mean? — is answered with a story rather than a rationale: we were slaves, and he brought us out, and commanded these things 'for our good always.' C14's household as the school in which the meaning of the law is handed down, and handed down as a memory of deliverance.

entries.pericope: You were the fewest of all peoples
entries.connection: The choice of Israel is explained by ruling out every reason that would flatter it: not because you were many, 'for you were the fewest of all peoples: but because Yahweh loves you.' Love that precedes merit, and a God who keeps covenant 'to a thousand generations.' C19's door is the same door — opened before anyone qualified to walk through it.

entries.pericope: That he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart
entries.connection: The forty years are read as a test 'to know what was in your heart' — pressure that reveals rather than creates, which is C21's diagnostic principle that what comes out under strain is inventory. The lesson of the manna is C18's: 'man does not live by bread only.' And the forty years themselves, with clothing that did not wear out, are C25's long formation, measured in decades rather than days.

entries.pericope: My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth
entries.connection: The second warning against abundance, more exact than the first: when the houses are built and the silver and gold multiplied, 'your heart be lifted up, and you forget,' and you say in your heart that you made this yourself. 'Remember Yahweh your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth.' C18's detachment as an accurate account of where wealth comes from. PR28 is not tagged; the danger named is pride and forgetting, not the use of the surplus.

entries.pericope: Not for your righteousness
entries.connection: Before success comes, the interpretation of it is forbidden: 'Don't say in your heart… For my righteousness Yahweh has brought me in.' Said three times, and ended with 'you are a stiff-necked people.' C04's mirror held up before a victory rather than after a failure, and C22's relational humility in its national form.

entries.pericope: I fell down before Yahweh forty days and forty nights
entries.connection: The golden calf retold, and Moses' part in it: the tablets broken, the calf ground to dust, and forty days face down interceding for a people who had 'quickly turned aside' — and for Aaron, who made the calf. 'Yahweh listened to me that time also.' Then the tablets are cut again and written 'according to the first writing,' and the journey resumes. C16's authority as standing between the weak and what they deserve; C19's door, reopened after the worst failure in the people's history. PR29 was considered, since the covenant is restored in full rather than on probation, but the text records Moses' intercession rather than the people's repentance, which the practice requires.

entries.pericope: Circumcise the foreskin of your heart… love the foreigner
entries.connection: 'What does Yahweh your God require of you' — the question Micah 6:8 will answer with the three pillars is asked first here. The answer reaches the heart: 'circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart,' the inward reading of the sign that C06 takes from Jeremiah 4:4 and that Jeremiah takes from this verse. Then the character of God as the ground of conduct: he 'executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and loves the foreigner, in giving him food and clothing. Therefore love the foreigner.' Provision for the stranger, the fatherless and the widow is how the Scriptural Appendix grounds Habitual Almsgiving in the Torah, and the reason given — 'for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt' — is C16's.

entries.pericope: Lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside
entries.connection: The land is described as one 'which Yahweh your God cares for: the eyes of Yahweh your God are always on it, from the beginning of the year even to the end of the year,' and its rain is tied to faithfulness. The moral order of C01 extended to weather. The warning is aimed at the heart before the act — 'take heed to yourselves, lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside' — which is C20's.

entries.pericope: You shall lay up these my words in your heart
entries.connection: The Shema's means repeated almost word for word: on the heart, on the hand, on the doorposts, taught to children when sitting, walking, lying down, rising. The repetition is itself the point — C28's formation by return. The practice tag is carried once, at 6:1-9.

entries.pericope: Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse
entries.connection: The Two Ways set out for the first time in the book, 'this day,' and fixed to two mountains so that the choice has a geography. C01's opening — reality has a grain, and choices go with it or against it — is this passage. Its fullest statement comes at 30:15-20, which the Scriptural Appendix cites and which will carry the prior when chapters 27-30 are indexed.

entries.pericope: You shall rejoice… you and your households… and the Levite who is within your gates
entries.connection: Worship in the law code begins with a meal and a command to rejoice, and the table is set wide: sons, daughters, male and female servants, and the Levite, 'because he has no portion nor inheritance with you.' 'Take heed to yourself that you don't forsake the Levite as long as you live in your land.' C10's delight, kept inside C14's household, with C16's insistence on the one who has no share of his own.

entries.pericope: How do these nations serve their gods? I will do likewise
entries.connection: The danger is placed at the moment of curiosity, before any act: 'take heed to yourself that you not be ensnared… and that you not inquire after their gods, saying, How do these nations serve their gods? I will do likewise.' The thought is quoted as it arrives, which is the attention C20 asks for.

entries.pericope: If the sign or the wonder come to pass
entries.connection: The test of a prophet is not whether his sign comes true. A prophet whose wonder happens exactly as predicted is still not to be heard if he leads 'after other gods,' and the sign is read as a test of the hearers' love. C08's fruit test in its sharpest form: what a teacher leads toward outweighs what he can do. The sentence that follows (13:5) and the laws of 13:6-18 are not indexed; see the coverage note.

entries.pericope: The foreigner, and the fatherless, and the widow… shall come, and shall eat and be satisfied
entries.connection: Two tithes. The yearly one is eaten before God with rejoicing — turned into money if the way is far and spent 'for whatever your soul desires.' The third-year tithe is laid up in the towns for those with no portion: the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, the widow, who 'shall eat and be satisfied.' A fixed share of increase, on a schedule, directed to actual need: Habitual Almsgiving as law, and the Torah's provision for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow that the Scriptural Appendix names as the practice's ground.

entries.pericope: Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart
entries.connection: The year of release, and the most searching law in the book about giving. 'You shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother.' Then the thought before the refusal is named: 'Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand' — the calculation that the loan will be cancelled — 'and your eye be evil against your poor brother, and you give him nothing.' Watchfulness catches a thought at the gate before it hardens into action; this law quotes the thought and tells you to catch it. And the giving itself reaches the heart: 'your heart shall not be grieved when you give.' 'The poor will never cease out of the land: therefore… you shall surely open your hand' makes almsgiving a permanent rhythm rather than a response to an emergency.

entries.pericope: You shall not let him go empty
entries.connection: A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year, and not empty-handed: 'you shall furnish him liberally out of your flock, and out of your threshing floor, and out of your winepress; as Yahweh your God has blessed you, you shall give to him.' Giving proportioned to one's own blessing, and grounded in memory: 'you shall remember that you were a bondservant.' The law regulates an institution the index does not commend; what it anchors is the command to send the departing away provided for, and 'it shall not seem hard to you.'

entries.pericope: You shall rejoice in your feast, you… and the foreigner, and the fatherless, and the widow
entries.connection: Three feasts a year, each a remembering — the bread of affliction eaten 'that you may remember the day when you came forth out of the land of Egypt all the days of your life' — and each a rejoicing to which the household's margins are named one by one: servants, the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, the widow. C28's formation by a rhythm of return, and C10's joy, made communal. PR25 shares the subject of the poor at the table, but nothing here is someone giving up their own seat, and it is not tagged.

entries.pericope: A bribe does blind the eyes of the wise
entries.connection: Judges in every gate, no partiality, no bribe — 'for a bribe does blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.' Interest corrupts perception before it corrupts judgment: the wise are blinded, not merely tempted. That is C07's claim that the lens is clouded by the condition of the one looking. 'That which is altogether just you shall follow' is C16's charge to those who hold power.

entries.pericope: That his heart not be lifted up above his brothers
entries.connection: The only law of kingship in the Torah limits the king rather than empowering him: not many horses, not many wives, not much silver and gold. And he is to write out a copy of the law and read it 'all the days of his life… that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers.' Authority constrained in what it may accumulate and kept level with those it governs is C16's argument, and the limit on accumulation is C18's.

entries.pericope: Yahweh is their inheritance
entries.connection: The Levites receive no land: 'Yahweh is their inheritance.' A tribe whose portion is a relation rather than a possession is C18's detachment as a social arrangement, provided for by the gifts of the others.

entries.pericope: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet… like me
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix cites 18:15 as the promise of the True Prophet. The passage frames it twice: against divination and sorcery, the illegitimate ways of knowing the future, and with a test for the prophet who speaks presumptuously — 'if the thing doesn't follow, nor happen… you shall not be afraid of him.' 'You shall be perfect with Yahweh your God' (18:13) is the wholeness the Book of Steps will later call the Perfect.

entries.pericope: Lest the avenger of blood pursue the manslayer, while his heart is hot
entries.connection: The cities of refuge in full, with the case given: an axe head flies off the handle and kills a neighbour. The law distinguishes the killing from the heart behind it — 'he didn't hate him in time past' — which is C21's distinction between act and root. It provides a door, C19's, close enough to reach. And it names the danger on the other side precisely: the avenger 'while his heart is hot,' anger that cannot tell the difference, which is why C22 measures healing by what anger does.

entries.pericope: At the mouth of two witnesses… shall a matter be established
entries.connection: No conviction on one witness, and the false witness receives what he intended for his brother. A claim must be tested before it is believed, which is C08's posture toward every voice. The closing formula, 'eye for eye, tooth for tooth' (19:21), is a limit on courts rather than a licence for persons, and it is the line Matthew 5:38-39 answers with Non-Retaliation; no practice is tagged here.

entries.pericope: Let him go and return to his house
entries.connection: Before battle, the officers send home the man with a new house not yet dedicated, a vineyard not yet tasted, a betrothed wife not yet married — and the man who is afraid, 'lest his brother's heart melt as his heart.' The ordinary goods of a household are protected even from the nation's war. C14's household, given priority over the army. The war laws that follow (20:10-20) are not indexed.

entries.pericope: Our hands have not shed this blood… Forgive, Yahweh, your people
entries.connection: A body is found in the open country and no one knows who killed him. The elders of the nearest town take responsibility for a death they did not cause: they declare honestly that their hands did not shed this blood, and then they ask forgiveness anyway. C04's audit carried out by a community rather than a person, and C16's account of the responsibility that comes with standing nearest.

entries.pericope: He may not make the son of the beloved the firstborn before the son of the hated
entries.connection: A father's preference for one wife may not override the right of the unloved wife's son. The household's justice is protected from its affections. C14's household in order, with the order defending the one the head of the house would rather pass over.

entries.pericope: You shall not see your brother's donkey or his ox fallen down by the way, and hide yourself
entries.connection: A neighbour's ox astray, his donkey fallen on the road: 'you may not hide yourself.' Bring it back, keep it until he comes for it, help him lift it up. The law is aimed at the moment of seeing and looking away, and it makes the interruption on the road the duty. Spontaneous Service is pausing your own work to help someone finish theirs, with the interruption treated as the actual work; this is its earliest form, and its failure named exactly — hiding yourself from what you have seen.

entries.pericope: You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you lived as a foreigner in his land
entries.connection: Of all the nations, the Egyptian — the enslaver of the exodus — is not to be abhorred, and the reason given is not his merit but Israel's memory: 'you lived as a foreigner in his land.' The Citizen-Stranger's practice includes a specific discipline: identify a group you have permitted yourself to despise, and lay down the contempt. This is that discipline commanded about the one group with the best claim to it. The circle is widened (C27) to include the third generation in the assembly. The verses immediately before, which exclude the Moabite 'forever' (23:3-6), are not indexed; the book of Ruth, whose heroine is a Moabite, is the canon's own reply to them.

entries.pericope: You shall not deliver to his master a servant who is escaped
entries.connection: A slave who escapes is not returned. He is to live 'in the place which he shall choose… where it pleases him best: you shall not oppress him.' The law sides with the one fleeing against the one with the claim, and gives him the choice of where to live. C16's why-the-vulnerable-specifically, in one of the most countercultural laws of the ancient world.

entries.pericope: That which is gone out of your lips you shall observe and do
entries.connection: There is no sin in not vowing; there is sin in vowing and not paying. What has left the lips is to be done. C13 is built around a vow kept, Ruth's, and this is the law beneath it: the vow is optional and the keeping is not.

entries.pericope: He shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer his wife
entries.connection: A newly married man is exempt from war and from public business for a year, and the purpose is stated: to 'cheer his wife whom he has taken.' The household's joy given legal priority over the nation's needs. C14's ordinary faithfulness, written into the calendar.

entries.pericope: In his day you shall give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down on it
entries.connection: Two laws with the same deadline. A lender may not enter a poor man's house to take his pledge, and if the pledge is his cloak it goes back before nightfall, 'that he may sleep in his garment.' The hired worker is paid the same day, 'neither shall the sun go down on it; for he is poor, and sets his heart on it.' The Scriptural Appendix names the wage paid before sundown as one of the Torah's grounds for Habitual Almsgiving. Mercy measured in hours, with the day as the unit of obligation that C28 makes the unit of formation.

entries.pericope: It shall be for the foreigner, for the fatherless, and for the widow
entries.connection: Justice for the foreigner and the fatherless, the widow's cloak not taken in pledge, and the gleaning laws: the forgotten sheaf left in the field, the olive boughs not beaten twice, the vineyard not gleaned 'after yourselves.' The Scriptural Appendix names the law of gleanings as a ground of Habitual Almsgiving, and it is the law under which Ruth gleans in Boaz's field — C13's three pillars in a barley field. Twice: 'you shall remember that you were a bondservant in the land of Egypt.'

entries.pericope: Lest your brother should seem vile to you
entries.connection: A guilty man may be beaten, but not beyond forty stripes, and the reason is not his body but his standing in the community's eyes: 'lest… your brother should seem vile to you.' Punishment is capped so that it does not turn the offender into something contemptible — he remains 'your brother' in the same sentence that sentences him. Merciful Reintegration exists so that a failure does not become a person's permanent identity. Confidence is medium: the law limits punishment rather than describing restoration after repentance, but its stated purpose is the practice's.

entries.pericope: So shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house
entries.connection: The duty of the brother-in-law to a childless widow, and the public shame of the man who refuses it. The law is the background of Ruth 4, where the nearer kinsman declines and Boaz accepts. PR26 is not tagged: the brother is obligated by law, and the practice is loyalty where one is free to walk away. What the passage anchors is C14 and C13 — a household's obligation to its most exposed member, and the cost of evading it.

entries.pericope: You shall have a perfect and just weight
entries.connection: No two weights in the bag, no two measures in the house, 'a great and a small' — one for buying and one for selling. The Scriptural Appendix names the honest scale as a ground of Habitual Almsgiving, and the tag follows the author. The drafter notes that the passage reads as naturally under the Moral Audit's examination of money and consistency, and that the connection to almsgiving is through the poor, who are always the ones measured with the false weight; a reviewer who reads it otherwise is disagreeing with WMT A3. C04's audit and C13's ordinary faithfulness in trade.

entries.pericope: A Syrian ready to perish was my father
entries.connection: The worshipper brings the first fruits and recites a story in which he is the beneficiary at every step: a perishing ancestor, affliction in Egypt, 'we cried to Yahweh… and Yahweh heard our voice, and saw our affliction.' Then 'you shall rejoice in all the good… you, and the Levite, and the foreigner.' Gratitude as a spoken memory of having been rescued, which is C10's discipline, and the cry heard which is C19's door.

entries.pericope: I have given them to the Levite, and to the foreigner, to the fatherless, and to the widow
entries.connection: At the end of the third-year tithe the giver makes a declaration before God: I have given it, according to the commandment; I have not forgotten. Giving followed by an honest account of the giving. Habitual Almsgiving with its accounting attached; the declaration resembles the Moral Audit's question about the vulnerable — whom did I help? — but is a vow fulfilled rather than an examination, so PR01 is not tagged.

entries.pericope: You have declared Yahweh this day to be your God… and Yahweh has declared you
entries.connection: The law code closes with a mutual declaration on the same day: the people declare Yahweh their God, and Yahweh declares them his people. The moral order of C01 presented as a covenant between persons rather than a code imposed from outside.

entries.pericope: Write on the stones all the words of this law very plainly
entries.connection: The law is to be written on plastered stones at the entrance to the land, 'very plainly,' beside an altar of uncut stone, and the people told: 'this day you have become the people of Yahweh your God.' A public, legible, checkable text at the threshold — C01's moral order set where everyone entering must pass it.

entries.pericope: Cursed is he who strikes his neighbor in secret
entries.connection: Twelve curses, each answered by the whole people with Amen. They gather on what is done out of sight: the image set up 'in secret,' the neighbour struck 'in secret,' the moved landmark, the blind led astray, the foreigner, fatherless, and widow deprived of justice. The community binds itself publicly against its own private conduct, which is the Moral Audit's question about consistency — where private conduct differs from public — said aloud by everyone at once. It is a covenant liturgy rather than an examination, so PR01 is not tagged; C04 carries the connection.

entries.pericope: You shall be blessed when you come in, and you shall be blessed when you go out
entries.connection: The blessings: city and field, body and ground, basket and kneading trough, coming in and going out. The claim is C01's — that conduct and consequence are not unrelated, that a life lived with the grain is blessed in its ordinary places. The book does not hide that the claim will be tested; Job and Ecclesiastes record the counter-evidence, and the index does not treat this chapter as a guarantee.

entries.pericope: Because you didn't serve Yahweh your God with joyfulness… by reason of the abundance of all things
entries.connection: The curses, longer and more detailed than the blessings, ending in exile and in a siege where the most refined man and woman in the city turn cruel toward their own families (28:53-57) — what comes out under pressure is inventory, as C21 says, and here it is described at its most terrible. One verse names the root: 'because you didn't serve Yahweh your God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, by reason of the abundance of all things.' Joyless obedience in plenty is given as the cause. C10's claim that delight belongs in a book of moral formation, and not as ornament, has its sternest warrant here. The siege passages are part of the pericope because they are part of the argument; they are not separately anchored.

entries.pericope: Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day
entries.connection: Forty years of signs, and the verdict: they saw the great wonders and were not given 'eyes to see.' Having witnessed is not the same as having perceived. C06 is built on the prayer of Psalm 119:18, open my eyes, because sight is given rather than achieved, and this is the sentence that makes the prayer necessary.

entries.pericope: Lest there should be among you a root that bears gall and wormwood
entries.connection: The covenant is made with everyone standing there — heads, elders, little ones, wives, the foreigner, 'from the one who cuts your wood to the one who draws your water' — and with those not yet born. C13's community, which includes its least members by name. Then a warning aimed at the interior: a 'root that bears gall,' the person who hears the curse and 'bless[es] himself in his heart, saying, I shall have peace, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart.' Failure traced to a root and a private reassurance, which is C21's anatomy; PR02 shares the image but the passage warns rather than prescribes the tracing, and it is not tagged.

entries.pericope: The secret things belong to Yahweh our God; but the things that are revealed belong to us
entries.connection: One verse divides knowledge in two: the hidden things are God's, and the revealed things are 'ours and our children's forever, that we may do all the words of this law.' The Discipline of Unknowing says it is not indecision — that one can act steadfastly while knowing one's understanding is partial. This verse is that sentence in its oldest form: what is not given is left with God, and what is given is for doing.

entries.pericope: Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart
entries.connection: After the curse, return: from the farthest exile, 'from there will Yahweh your God gather you.' The change that 10:16 commanded — circumcise your heart — is now promised as God's own act: 'Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart… to love Yahweh your God.' C19's door from the far country, and C26's change of nature by gift, the promise Ezekiel 36:26 will repeat.

entries.pericope: It is not too hard for you, neither is it far off
entries.connection: The commandment is neither in heaven nor beyond the sea; 'the word is very near to you, in your mouth, and in your heart, that you may do it.' C05's insistence that the road be walkable — 'do what you are able' — answered from the law's side: it was never meant to be out of reach. And the word in the heart is C11's indwelling in its Old Testament form, which Paul will quote in Romans 10.

entries.pericope: Therefore choose life
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix cites 30:19 as the Two Ways in God's own words: life and good, death and evil, set before you 'this day' — 'therefore choose life.' C01 begins here. The Daily Anchors begin each morning with the same choice spoken aloud, 'today I choose the Way of Life,' and the passage makes the choice daily, repeated, and concrete: love, obey, cling, 'for he is your life, and the length of your days.' This is where the practice's morning sentence comes from.

entries.pericope: He will not fail you, nor forsake you
entries.connection: A man of a hundred and twenty who can 'no more go out and come in' hands on his work in public, and his last charge to his successor is encouragement: be strong, don't be afraid, 'he will not fail you, neither forsake you.' Authority laid down for the sake of the one who takes it up, C16's, and growth across a span longer than one life, C25's.

entries.pericope: That their children, who have not known, may hear, and learn
entries.connection: Every seventh year at the feast of tents the whole law is read aloud to everyone — men, women, little ones, the foreigner — 'that they may hear, and that they may learn.' Formation by scheduled return to the same text, C28's rhythm, and the household of C14 extended to the whole people with the children named as the point.

entries.pericope: I know their imagination which they frame this day
entries.connection: God tells Moses that the people will turn away, and gives a song to be their witness 'for it shall not be forgotten out of the mouths of their seed.' The failure is foreseen — 'I know their imagination which they frame this day, before I have brought them into the land' — and provision is made in advance for the moment they are ready to recognise it. C21's reading of the heart before the act, and C19's door built before the fall rather than after it.

entries.pericope: The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice
entries.connection: The Scriptural Appendix cites 32:4 for the claim that God's ways are justice — that the moral order and the divine character are one thing seen from two angles, which is C01's foundation. The song then tells what that character did: found a people 'in the waste howling wilderness,' kept him 'as the apple of his eye,' as an eagle stirs her nest and bears her young on her wings. The justice and the care belong to the same Rock, which is the ground of C19's hope.

entries.pericope: Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked
entries.connection: The prosperity of the first half produces the apostasy of the second: 'Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked… Then he forsook God who made him.' C18's warning about abundance in its most compressed form. The lament at the centre — 'Oh that they were wise, that they understood this, that they would consider their latter end!' — is C02's first truth, seeing the end of the path. 'Vengeance is mine, and recompense' (32:35) is the verse Paul quotes in Romans 12:19 when he tells his readers not to avenge themselves; here it is God's declaration about his adversaries rather than an instruction to anyone, and the anchor for Paul's use of it belongs at Romans.

entries.pericope: It is no vain thing for you; because it is your life
entries.connection: Moses' last word on the law — 'it is no vain thing for you; because it is your life' — and then the command to climb Nebo and die there, seeing the land and not entering, because of Meribah. The law as life is C01; the consequence that stands even after forty years of faithful service, accepted without protest, is C18's freedom from the one thing he wanted.

entries.pericope: The eternal God is your dwelling place. Underneath are the everlasting arms
entries.connection: From the blessing of the tribes, the one line that reaches beyond them: God as a dwelling place, and underneath, the everlasting arms. C09's secret place and C11's remaining are both spatial images of being held, and this is their Old Testament root. The rest of the tribal blessings (33:1-25, 28-29) are not indexed; they bless particular tribes and anchor nothing in personal formation. 27b ('Destroy!') belongs to the conquest material and is not what the entry anchors.

entries.pericope: No man knows of his tomb to this day
entries.connection: The greatest prophet in Israel dies outside the land, is buried by God, and 'no man knows of his tomb to this day.' His eye was not dim; the people wept thirty days, and then 'the days of weeping in the mourning for Moses were ended.' A life given to a promise he would not personally enter, ending in a grave no one could make into a monument. C23's hidden life at its most literal, and C18's detachment completed.
